statement: Two sides of a triangle are 4 cm and 9 cm long. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. How many different lengths are possible for the third side?

choices.misconception: I thought the third side had to be the longest side, so I only counted 10, 11 and 12.
I took 13 - 5 = 8, counting the gap between the limits instead of the whole numbers strictly between them.
I included 5 and 13 as well, but those lengths make the triangle collapse flat.
I only checked that the third side was shorter than 4 + 9, so I counted every length from 1 to 12.

hints: Could the third side be 1 cm long? Could it be 20 cm?
Each side must be shorter than the other two added together. That gives an upper limit from the sum and a lower limit from the difference, and neither limit itself is allowed.
The third side must be more than 9 - 4 = 5 and less than 9 + 4 = 13.

solutions.reliable: The triangle inequality says the third side c must satisfy 9 - 4 < c < 9 + 4, that is 5 < c < 13. The whole numbers strictly between are 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12, which is 7 lengths. At exactly 5 or 13 the three points would lie on one straight line. The transferable idea: the third side of a triangle lies strictly between the difference and the sum of the other two.
solutions.elegant: Fix the 9 cm side and let the 4 cm side swing on a hinge at one end. The gap it leaves grows smoothly from 5 cm, folded flat, to 13 cm, opened flat, and every length strictly in between makes a real triangle. So count the whole numbers from 6 to 12.

whyOnTest: The triangle inequality is a one-step check, and the choices punish the usual slips: counting the flat cases and checking only one end of the range.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
